analysis.one_liner: Phases out for-profit prisons, caps prison phone fees, ends the ICE detention bed quota, and reinstates federal parole.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees and three subcommittees but never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required federal, state, and local governments to run adult prisons and detention centers directly instead of paying private companies to do it, with limited waivers. It would have reinstated parole for federal prisoners sentenced after the bill's enactment, capped what companies charge prisoners and their families for phone, video, and money-transfer services, and directed the FCC to limit the fees prisons collect from phone providers. It also would have removed the requirement that Immigration and Customs Enforcement keep at least 34,000 detention beds available, ended family detention, and required annual inspections of all immigration detention facilities.
analysis.who_benefits: People incarcerated in federal and state prisons, immigrant detainees and their families, and the relatives who pay for their phone calls and money transfers. Federal prisoners would regain a path to early release through parole after serving roughly a third of their sentences [S2][S3]. Families paying prison phone and money-transfer fees would pay rates capped at reasonable, cost-based levels [S2][S3]. Immigrant families would no longer be detained or separated as family units, and detention would be sized to actual needs rather than a guaranteed 34,000-bed quota [S2][S3]. Taxpayers would no longer pay to guarantee empty or filled private detention beds regardless of need [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Prisoners, immigrant detainees, and their families

how_it_helps.text: Within two years, every federal adult prison and detention facility would have to be under direct government control with government employees performing core correctional services, and states and localities would be barred from contracting out prison operations, with waivers available for up to one extra year [S3].
Federal prisoners sentenced on or after the bill's enactment would become eligible for parole after serving about one-third of their term, restoring a release mechanism abolished in 1984 [S2][S3].

The FCC would have to cap per-minute and per-call rates for prison phone and video service, require collect and debit calling options, prohibit or limit the commission payments prisons receive from phone companies, allow competing providers, and limit add-on fees [S2][S3].
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would set rules requiring fees for sending money to inmates and detainees to be reasonable and proportional to the actual cost of the service [S2][S3].

The mandatory 34,000-bed ICE detention quota would be repealed, detention capacity would be set by actual need, nationwide alternatives-to-detention programs would be created, and family detention and family separation for detention purposes would be prohibited except for parents deemed dangerous on terrorism grounds [S2][S3].

All immigration detention facilities would face annual government inspections and biennial independent audits, unannounced oversight, financial penalties for substandard performance, and contract termination for repeat violators; detained people would get a private right to sue with damages of at least $1,000 per violation [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private prison companies would lose federal, state, and local contracts worth billions of dollars, and their stock-market investors would bear that loss. Prison phone and video providers would lose high per-minute rates and the commission payments they make to prison administrators, and money-transfer companies would lose inflated fees. State and local governments would need to resume directly operating facilities or absorb facilities as contracts end, and federal agencies would need to hire staff and expand government-run capacity during the transition.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison and prison telecom companies

drawbacks.text: The two-year deadlines include a one-year waiver if the Attorney General finds governments cannot comply, so the ban on private prisons could be extended rather than firm [S3].

Transitioning facilities to government operation would require public spending on staff, facilities, and the federal Parole Commission, which the bill would make permanent; critics of government-run systems argue public prisons carry their own cost and oversight problems.

Reinstating parole would give an appointed Parole Commission discretion to release prisoners after serving a portion of their sentences, which opponents of early-release mechanisms argue reduces sentence certainty for victims and courts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — ending the practice of governments paying companies to run prisons and to charge captive customers for phones and money transfers — goes directly to incarcerated people, detained families, and the relatives who foot the bills, at a real but transitional cost to governments building replacement capacity. The parole provision is the broadest and most contested piece, since it changes sentencing outcomes for an entire category of federal prisoners and depends on how a re-created Parole Commission exercises its discretion. The bill's one-year waiver for the private-prison ban is a genuine weakness, but the fee caps and detention reforms are specific and enforceable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to four House committees when introduced and split among three subcommittees, but none of them ever took it up, and it died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on July 13, 2017, joined by 10 original cosponsors [S1][S3].
It was referred to the Judiciary, Financial Services, Energy and Commerce, and Homeland Security Committees [S5].

Within a month it was referred to three subcommittees — Communications and Technology, Border and Maritime Security, and Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations — and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
All 52 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill never reached a committee markup or a floor vote in either chamber, and it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private prison operators, prison phone and video providers, and money-transfer companies kept their government contracts and their revenue from fees charged to inmates' families. The private prison industry also saw policy move its way during this period, as the Trump administration reversed a 2016 Obama-era plan to phase out federal private prison contracts — widely reported and outside the provided sources.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private prison and prison phone companies

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 53 supporters — the sponsor plus 52 cosponsors — was a Democrat, and the Republican-controlled House never acted on it; no roll-call vote was ever taken [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Private prison and detention facility operators
industries.note: The bill would phase out federal contracts for privately run adult prisons within two years and bar private entities from operating state and local adult prisons, forcing companies like CoreCivic and GEO Group out of their core government business. These companies profit from per-bed government payments for incarcerating people, so their financial interest runs directly against the detainees the bill would move into government-run facilities.

industries.industry: Prison phone and video service providers
industries.note: The FCC would have to cap per-minute and connection rates, ban or limit the commissions these companies pay to prisons (a cost passed on to families), allow competing providers, and limit add-on fees. These companies currently earn high rates from a captive customer base of prisoners and their relatives.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would require fees for sending money to inmates and detainees to be reasonable and proportional to actual cost, cutting fees that currently exceed the cost of the service for families sending funds to incarcerated loved ones.

industries.industry: Government corrections and immigration enforcement agencies
industries.note: Federal, state, and local agencies would take on the cost and staffing of running facilities directly and would lose commission revenue from phone contracts, but they would gain flexibility by shedding the mandatory 34,000-bed ICE detention quota and gaining alternatives-to-detention tools.
